Title: Greek parents brace for back-to-school spending season

Footfall in bookshops and school supply stores is already rising, as parents search for notebooks, stationery, art materials and the rest of the gear pupils will need.
The return to the classroom is approaching, and with it the usual budget exercise for Greek families, who must buy everything their children need for the new school year.
Footfall in bookshops and stores selling school supplies has already started to pick up, with parents looking for exercise books, stationery, art materials and all the other equipment pupils will need.
Prices for basic products are, by and large, close to last year's levels. The final cost, however, can differ significantly depending on the pupil's year group, the school's list, the quality of the products and whether parents opt for branded or more economical items.
According to a market survey by Ertnews Radio 105.8, the cost of basic school supplies for a child in the first years of primary school is estimated at around €100 to €120 this year. This does not include the school bag, lunch box, food container or water bottle.
From €15 to €100 for a school bag
The gap between the cheapest and the most expensive options remains wide.
A school bag can start at around €15, while more expensive or branded models can cost as much as €100.
A classic blue 50-page exercise book starts at around €0.49, while a maths notebook costs between €1.59 and €2.50. Writing notebooks range from roughly €0.80 to €2.
The spread is even wider for two-subject spiral notebooks, which can cost between €1 and €8.
In art supplies, a pad of watercolour paper starts at about €2.25 and can go up to €15, with the average price around €3.50. A set of 12 felt-tip pens, as well as a set of brushes, starts at around €2.50, while the more expensive options can reach €10.
What parents paid in 2025
The comparison with prices recorded a year earlier is also revealing. In September 2025, the Greek Workers' Consumers Association (EEKE) published specific prices for a series of basic school products, following a sample survey of supermarket chains.
In 2025, a 17x24cm two-subject spiral notebook cost €1.64, while an A4 two-subject spiral notebook cost €2.55. A set of 12 fine washable felt-tip pens cost €1.99, and another set of 12 felt-tip pens cost €1.89. A pack of five pencils cost €1.49, four pens cost €1.29, and a compass with a pencil cost €1.49. A set of sharpener and eraser cost €0.99, a 20-centimetre ruler cost €0.36, and a pack of 12 coloured pencils cost €2.85.
These figures are not fully comparable with every product on the shelves this year, as the brand, packaging, dimensions or point of sale may differ. They do, however, give a picture of the level at which basic school supplies were priced in 2025.
It is also worth noting that on 28 August 2025, the Ministry of Development announced, after a meeting with the Hellenic Supermarkets Association, that companies had pledged to keep the prices of school supplies at their 2024 levels.
The ministry's official announcement did not, however, include detailed prices for each product code.
A year on, the picture suggests that in many categories the lowest prices remain at relatively affordable levels. The wide gap between budget and more expensive options, though, means the final bill can easily climb.
For a family with two or more school-age children, even small differences in the price of each item add up, turning preparations for the first day of school into a significant expense for the household budget.

Title: Can Dimple Yadav broaden SP appeal in 2027 challenge to BJP?

In contemporary Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party (SP) is no longer merely the principal opposition party. Its president, Akhilesh Yadav, has emerged as one of the most formidable challengers to the Narendra Modi-led BJP government after Congress leader Rahul Gandhi. His sharp, often acerbic, attacks on the Modi government frequently go viral, while his press conferences in Lucknow have become a regular platform for taking on the Adityanath government.
Akhilesh has always had a combative political style. But the SP’s strong performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election appears to have given him a renewed confidence. His attacks on both the Modi and the Adityanath governments have since become sharper and more pointed.
The 2024 general election was a particularly significant turning point because the SP won 37 of Uttar Pradesh’s 80 Lok Sabha seats, while the Congress won six. The BJP won 33 seats, while the Rashtriya Lok Dal won two and Apna Dal (Soneylal) and the Azad Samaj Party won one each. Thus, the INDIA bloc won 43 seats in the State, against 36 for the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA).
The Uttar Pradesh result played a crucial role in creating a setback for the BJP on the national stage, when it had hoped to win at least 400 seats in the Lok Sabha. Instead, it was reduced to 240 seats, falling short of a majority on its own and able to cross the majority mark only with its allies and forming government as the NDA.
The SP’s victory in Faizabad, the constituency that includes the Ayodhya seat, was particularly damaging to the BJP’s political narrative. Coming just months after the inauguration of the Ram temple, the result was widely interpreted as a symbolic setback for Hindutva politics. Akhilesh further underlined the symbolism by prominently seating Faizabad MP Awadhesh Prasad beside him in Parliament, a political gesture designed to send a broader message: that the seemingly inexorable rise of Hindutva politics since 2014 could be facing a political correction.
2027, the real test for Akhilesh
The Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, expected in early 2027, will nevertheless pose a much tougher challenge for Akhilesh. The SP has been out of power in the State for a decade, while Adityanath has emerged as one of the BJP’s most powerful political figures.
There is already speculation in political circles that another term as Chief Minister could strengthen Adityanath’s position as a potential contender for the BJP’s top leadership position after the 2029 Lok Sabha election. In that context, the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election is not merely another State contest. It could have implications for the BJP’s larger political succession and national strategy.
Adityanath’s strongest political narrative has been built around governance, particularly law and order. The opposition, however, has consistently challenged the government’s claims on this front, including its methods of policing. National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data has provided the opposition with ammunition to question the government’s broader law-and-order narrative.
According to NCRB data, registered cases of serious offences increased from 64,450 in 2017, when the SP was ousted from power, to 85,647 in 2024. The same argument extends to crimes against women: the number of registered cases rose from 56,011 in 2017 to 66,398 in 2024.
However, the BJP, despite these statistics, has repeatedly succeeded in putting the SP on the defensive on the question of law and order, particularly on women’s security. The party’s ability to associate the SP with the old “lawlessness” narrative remains one of its most potent political weapons.
Enter Dimple Yadav
This is precisely where Dimple Yadav, Mainpuri MP and Akhilesh’s spouse, could become important to the SP’s 2027 strategy. Akhilesh appears to be increasingly positioning her at the centre of the party’s public campaign.
Her recent political interventions suggest that this is more than a matter of occasional joint appearances. Dimple was very visible during the Jantar Mantar protest, comforting injured students, offering assistance, and engaging with their concerns.
She has also been increasingly vocal in Parliament on issues such as paper leaks and matters concerning students. Her increasingly frequent presence alongside Akhilesh at press conferences further strengthens the impression that she could become one of the SP’s principal campaign faces in 2027.
Her joint press conference with Akhilesh in Lucknow on the party’s proposed Stree Samman Samriddhi Yojana was particularly revealing. It offered a glimpse of how the SP could attempt to make women’s issues a central component of its electoral messaging in the upcoming election. (The SP announced on August 26 that if it came to power, it would implement the scheme under which women would receive Rs.40,000 every year to help them become economically stronger.)
The political logic behind the strategy is straightforward. For years, the BJP has successfully attacked the SP through the lens of law and order, particularly by invoking the image of the “gunda raj” associated with previous SP governments. Dimple offers the party a way to change the tone and perhaps even the terms of that debate.
Her political persona is markedly different from the traditional image associated with the SP. She has a relatively restrained, composed, and articulate public image. That allows the party to present a different face to voters—particularly women, urban voters, and younger sections of the electorate.
More importantly, Dimple can potentially turn the BJP’s strongest line of attack into an area of political contestation. Instead of allowing the BJP to exclusively define the women’s security debate, the SP can use Dimple to ask a counter-question: if the BJP claims to have transformed law and order and made Uttar Pradesh safer for women, what do the NCRB numbers say?
That does not automatically make the argument electorally successful. But it changes the debate. And that may be precisely what the SP wants.
The 2022 Assembly election demonstrated the BJP’s continuing strength. The party won 273 seats, comfortably securing a majority, while the SP won 111. But the 2024 Lok Sabha results produced a dramatically different electoral map. If the Lok Sabha results are mapped onto Assembly segments, the INDIA bloc led in 224 Assembly segments, compared with 174 for the NDA—a difference of 50 segments. Within the INDIA bloc, the SP led in 184 segments and the Congress in 39, while the Trinamool Congress led in one segment. On the NDA side, the BJP led in 162 segments, the RLD in eight, and Apna Dal (S) in four.
However, these figures should not be read as a direct forecast of the 2027 Assembly election. Lok Sabha and Assembly elections are fought on different issues, with different candidate equations and different turnout patterns. But they are nevertheless a warning signal for the BJP. They demonstrate that the electoral arithmetic that produced a comfortable BJP majority in 2022 is no longer as secure as it once appeared.
The Gen Z challenge
There is another constituency that could prove particularly important in 2027: young voters. The BJP has traditionally enjoyed considerable appeal among first-time and younger voters. But the political mood among sections of Gen Z appears far more fluid than it was a decade ago.
Recent youth protests and student mobilisations have demonstrated that issues such as employment, examinations, paper leaks, recruitment scams, and a lack of educational opportunities can generate political anger that go beyond traditional caste and ideological boundaries. The size of this electorate makes the issue impossible to ignore.
According to the Election Commission of India’s publication titled Atlas 2024, 21.19 per cent of Uttar Pradesh’s electors were between 18 and 29 as of May 20, 2024, which is roughly one in every five voters. The all-India figure was 22.78 per cent. For the 2027 Assembly election, therefore, this young electorate segment could become a decisive political constituency.
This is another area where Dimple’s role could matter. Her relatively modern public persona, her engagement with student issues, and her increasing visibility on questions concerning women and young people could give the SP a political bridge to voters who may not necessarily identify with the party’s traditional social base.
The question, therefore, is not whether Dimple will campaign in 2027. She almost certainly will. The more important question is how central a role will the SP give her, and whether the party can convert her personal appeal into an electoral asset.
Akhilesh remains the undisputed political face and decision-maker of the SP. But Dimple can complement his political persona rather than compete with it. Where Akhilesh is combative, Dimple can be conciliatory. Where he attacks, she can empathise. While he speaks to the government, she can speak to citizens. That combination could prove politically useful.
The BJP will still have considerable advantages: powerful organisational machinery, strong ideological network, Modi’s popularity, Adityanath’s personal political appeal, and finally, a well-established electoral coalition. But the SP enters 2027 with something it did not possess in the same measure before 2024: political momentum and confidence.
Dimple’s emergence as a prominent campaign face, combined with the concerns of a large young electorate, could give that momentum a new dimension.
The 2027 election, therefore, may not simply be a contest between Akhilesh and Adityanath. It could also become a contest over which political narrative speaks more convincingly to Uttar Pradesh’s women and its young voters.
If Dimple succeeds in making these two constituencies part of the SP’s political conversation, she could turn out to be far more important than just being Akhilesh’s campaign companion. She could become one of the defining faces of the SP’s 2027 challenge to the BJP.

Title: All eyes on Fed Chair Warsh during the central bank’s annual conclave in Jackson Hole

Fed Chair Warsh signals rate hikes may be needed with inflation still elevated
Watch live as Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first high-profile speech at the central bank’s annual conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
JACKSON HOLE, Wyoming (AP) — Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Friday that inflation is still too high and suggested the central bank may have to raise interest rates in the coming months to bring it down, a clearer signal than he had sent previously about his economic outlook.
In his first high-profile speech at the Fed’s annual conference at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Warsh acknowledged that recent U.S. data show inflation has cooled a bit, but “they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” Warsh said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”
The Fed chair, who replaced his predecessor, Jerome Powell on May 22, faces high stakes with his speech as questions swirl around Wall Street about his focus on fighting inflation.
Those concerns may have contributed to rising bond yields, which can increase the cost of borrowing for the government and everyone else. Yet Warsh has said he doesn’t want to provide what analysts call “forward guidance” about whether the Fed will hike or cut rates or stay on hold at upcoming meetings. He argues that it limits the Fed’s flexibility by committing it to a specific policy.
Yet some economists have argued that he could say more about his views on Fed policy without tipping his hand about future actions.
Warsh on Friday reiterated his skepticism about providing such guidance or even outlining his broad approach to interest-rate policy.
But he did suggest that interest rates currently aren’t restricting economic activity, pointing to robust business investment in AI equipment and infrastructure and strong consumer spending. As a rule of thumb, interest rates often need to be high enough to limit borrowing and spending to cool inflation.
The Fed next meets September 15-16, and Warsh’s remarks don’t necessarily signal the central bank will raise rates then. But his speech indicated that rates may not be high enough to bring inflation down to the Fed’s 2% target.
Warsh said inflation data “are more concerning” than trends on the job market, where the unemployment rate is low. He also argued that inflation is unlikely to move back to the target on its own.
Warsh noted that in the past year, 54% of goods and services tracked by the government have seen price increases of 3% or higher. While that is down from the pandemic peak, it is “well above” the 32% that saw such increases in the two decades before the pandemic.
Inflation cooled in June and July after spiking in May from soaring gas prices, yet it remains above the central bank’s target. According to the Fed’s preferred measure, it was 3.7% in July.
Warsh also sought to clear up some areas of confusion that arose after his remarks at a July 29 news conference. He specified that short-term interest rates are the “predominant tool” the Fed can use to lower inflation.
Previous Fed chairs have often used speeches at Jackson Hole to address broad questions about interest-rate policy and the economy, or to signal upcoming changes in their approach. In 2022, with pandemic-era inflation having soared to 9.1%, Warsh’s predecessor Powell signaled the Fed would continue to sharply raise interest rates in a fight against runaway prices, and he acknowledged that such maneuvers would bring “pain” to consumers and businesses.
Most analysts expect the Fed will keep rates unchanged when it meets next in mid-September. Wall Street investors, however, are betting the central bank will hike rates by December, according to futures pricing tracked by CME FedWatch.
Questions about Warsh’s approach have intensified amid President Donald Trump’s continued calls for lower interest rates. While Trump has continued to defend Warsh, whom he appointed, the president has criticized other Fed officials for supporting higher rates.
Trump has also renewed his efforts to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden. Replacing Cook would enable Trump to appoint a majority of the seven-member board. Trump tried to fire her last year but was temporarily blocked by the Supreme Court.
If Warsh does assuage some of these concerns, longer-term interest rates could decline slightly. Those rates have steadily risen in recent weeks because of a range of factors, including burgeoning U.S. government deficits and outsize borrowing by tech firms building AI infrastructure.
The rate on the 30-year Treasury bond reached the highest level in 19 years last week, prompting an unusual effort by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to buy back bonds and push the yields lower.

Title: What happens when information theory accounts for reasoning?

Imagine a cataclysm wipes out humanity's scientific knowledge. Hard drives, the internet, books, movies — all about to be lost. But before everything is gone, you have the chance to leave a single sentence for future generations. What would you write?
Physicist Richard Feynman once answered that hypothetical saying he would tell the future of humanity that all things are made of atoms. He believed that from that one sentence, an enormous amount of scientific knowledge could eventually be reconstructed.
Feynman’s sentence is so valuable not because of the number of words or symbols it contains, rather everything a future scientist could infer from it. For nearly 80 years, the field of information theory has largely focused on transmitting information efficiently, rather than accounting for what people can deduce from that information.
A new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) by IBM Research scientists Luis Lastras, Jonathan Lenchner, Barry Trager, Mark Squillante, Chai Wah Wu, Ronald Fagin, and collaborators Wojciech Szpankowski and Alexander Gray, proposes a new way of thinking about communication. It’s one that explicitly accounts for reasoning.
Shannon's simplification
In 1948, American scientist Claude Shannon transformed communications with a remarkably powerful idea. He realized that you could separate the meaning of a message from the problem of transmitting it efficiently.
That abstraction led to modern information theory. Whether the message is a photograph, a phone call, a scientific paper, this blog, or the training data for a large language model, Shannon's framework focuses on how information can be represented, compressed, and transmitted reliably. The approach proved successful because communication networks don't need to understand what they're carrying. The internet doesn't care whether a packet contains a life-saving medical diagnosis or a picture of a cat. It simply moves the bits.
Yet the humans at either end of a communication instinctively recognize that not all bits are equally valuable. A single bit generated by a faulty sensor may be worthless; a single bit from a reliable collision-avoidance system telling an autonomous vehicle to brake could be enormously valuable. The difference lies in what can be inferred from that information.
Bringing reasoning into the model
Lastras and his collaborators asked what would happen if communication systems explicitly accounted for logical deduction.
Their framework extends Shannon's classic sender-receiver model by giving the receiver a reasoning capability. Rather than measuring only the information that is transmitted directly, the model also considers the additional knowledge that can be derived from what was received.
The central insight the team arrived at is that communication becomes more efficient when reasoning is allowed. Instead of transmitting every fact individually, a sender can provide information that enables a receiver to infer many additional facts. In other words, the value of a message depends not only on what it says, but also on what it allows someone to conclude.
To capture this mathematically, the researchers derived a new quantity, called ‘logical semantic entropy,’ which defines the fundamental communication limits in the presence of reasoning capabilities.
A trio of theories
The team’s framework produced several results that challenge conventional intuition. One finding, which the researchers call the "No Need to Know" result, examines what happens when a sender doesn't know exactly what a receiver already knows. Surprisingly, they found that the fundamental communication limit remains essentially unchanged. This is unexpected because their communication inherently drops details unnecessary for logical deduction (using lossy compression) — a setting where knowing what the recipient already understands usually helps save data.
A second finding led to what they named the "Less Is More" paradox. They borrowed two fictional characters commonly used in cryptography theory, Alice and Bob. If Alice wants Bob to learn only a particular subset of her knowledge while using as few bits as possible, the most efficient strategy can end up teaching Bob more than intended. By using broad, pre-set shorthand patterns to solve multiple scenarios at once, Alice dramatically cuts down on the total data sent. However, because these patterns cover extra ground, sharing one necessarily reveals more background context to Bob than necessary, creating a potential security risk.
The researchers also explored a model for correcting mistaken beliefs. Their analysis suggests that the communication cost of correcting incorrect information can become dramatically larger than the cost of filling a simple knowledge gap. By mathematically modeling communication when a receiver holds beliefs that directly contradict the sender's facts, the researchers calculated the extra data cost required to correct someone who is wrong versus informing someone who is just unaware of the facts. They found that as the receiver becomes more specific and strongly opinionated in their incorrect beliefs, the relative cost to guide them back to the truth grows to infinity.
From side project to a larger conversation
For Lastras, the project wasn't a short-term initiative. The work began as a personal research effort pursued largely in the background with a small team. Over several years, he devoted time each week to exploring a question that had remained unresolved since the early days of information theory. That small team slowly grew as collaborators helped reach deeper into the field of mathematical logic to explore the topic in greater depth.
Modern AI systems increasingly depend not only on processing information, but also on reasoning over it. While Shannon's original framework remains the foundation of digital communication, Lastras and team argue that future intelligent systems may benefit from a richer theory that accounts for what can be inferred from information — not simply how efficiently that information can be transmitted.
In that sense, the paper extends a conversation that began in 1948 and asks a new question for the age of intelligent systems: What if communication theory measured not just the data sent, but the background knowledge required to make sense of it?

Title: Warsh, In Our Time

August 28, 2026 In Our Time At “Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy,” an economic policy symposium sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Jackson Hole, Wyoming Thank you. It's great to be here again and to see so many familiar faces. I've been looking forward to this weekend—what better place to mark my 100th day as Chairman? For the fine hospitality, everyone here is in debt to President Jeff Schmid and his colleagues at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City. Jeff, our thanks to you all. Jeff and the other planners have some recreation options lined up for later today. And I'd advise you to be very careful with your choices. As I learned years ago, you can take two different kinds of hikes on the trails around Jackson Hole. I can sum up my hikes with former Vice Chairman Don Kohn in two words: I survived. These steely marathon death marches revealed a side of Don I wasn't ready for. There's another kind of hike—one I associate with Chairman Ben Bernanke, my old colleague. With Ben, it's a much more leisurely pace, an easy stroll along the wandering trails at the Rockefeller Preserve. So before setting out, do a wellness check and ask yourself: "Is this a Kohn day or a Bernanke day?" The best thing about this gathering is that it helps us all clear our minds and think straight about our world and our time. For me, it feels like the right place, and the right audience, for a real engagement with the ideas that matter most. Innovation is the conference theme, and I believe that the public and the markets—in their collective wisdom—understand that innovations in the conduct of policy at the Fed will help deliver price stability alongside full employment. Here is a quick overview of what I'll cover in my remarks this morning. You can call it an outline . . . you can call it a trail map . . . just don't call it forward guidance. Title: NVIDIA Ising Enables Fully Automated Quantum Computer Calibration with Enhanced In-Context Learning

NVIDIA Ising Calibration is an open source vision language model (VLM) designed to interpret diagnostic outputs from quantum processors and determine how they should be tuned to continue operating.
This post introduces the latest model release, NVIDIA Ising Calibration 1.5, which advances AI-based QPU calibration by analyzing unfamiliar diagnostic results without prior training examples. Ising Calibration 1.5 also uses examples from related experiments when available and is 11.4% smaller at BF16 precision. This eases the deployment of agentic calibration workflows directly in local lab environments.
For the first time, the model is also available in an NVFP4-quantized version, enabling deployment on a single GPU or an NVIDIA DGX Spark—comparable with leading closed models such as Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol.
The Ising Calibration 1.5 model is trained on data generated from partner contributions across multiple qubit modalities, including superconducting qubits, quantum dots, ions, neutral atoms, electrons on Helium, and others specializing in calibration and control.
Performance of Ising Calibration 1.5 is evaluated using the QCalEval benchmark, which measures a model’s ability to interpret experimental results, classify outcomes, evaluate significance, assess fit quality and key features, and recommend next steps. For additional details on the benchmark, model architecture, and evaluation results, see QCalEval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Quantum Calibration Plot Understanding.
The evaluation covers both zero-shot and in-context learning (ICL). Zero-shot reasoning analyzes results independently, while ICL evaluates results in the context of related samples. Both are important for building agents that can automate QPU bring-up and retune operations.
On the QCalEval benchmark, Ising Calibration 1.5 shows strong performance when analyzing diagnostic results without prior examples. It is now also 86.68% better than its predecessor when using examples from related experiments. It outperforms comparable open models and remains competitive with leading closed models.
Ising Calibration 1.5 advances AI and quantum computing calibration by outperforming all open models out of the box and on the QCalEval benchmark. It is competitive with state-of-the-art closed or 1T+ parameter models.
The 31-billion-parameter VLM is suited for data center GPUs such as NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and NVIDIA Vera Rubin. It also ships with a quantized version to NVFP4 where users can run this model on a consumer gaming card or NVIDIA DGX Spark with only a small cost in accuracy.
The tokens per second (TPS) performance on DGX Spark has also been optimized, enabling good throughput locally for a fraction of the cost.
To learn more about deploying Ising Calibration 1.5 with an agent, check out the NVIDIA/Quantum-Calibration-Agent-Blueprint GitHub repo.
The NVIDIA Ising model family is fully open. Weights, data, benchmarks, and recipes are provided so you can modify, deploy, and fine-tune your own models and variants for your specific QPUs.
Full-parameter checkpoints for Ising Calibration 1.5 are available on Hugging Face:
Ising Calibration 1.5 is also available as an NVIDIA NIM and hosted through NVIDIA Build. The OpenMDW License from Linux Foundation offers QPU builders and operators with the flexibility to maintain data control and deploy anywhere.
A ready-to-use agent harness blueprint is available with support for this model and others, including large model cloud APIs.
- Quantum calibration agent blueprint is a script for deploying an agentic workflow using Ising Calibration 1.5 with the NVIDIA Nemo Agent Toolkit to quickly set up quantum calibration experiment automation.
Ising Calibration 1.5 is built on real QPU data provided by partners and collaborators. A semantic quantum calibration benchmark has also been released to evaluate model effectiveness for this task.

Title: Rescuers grapple with mountain of challenges after the Nepal-Tibet floods

Rescuers grapple with mountain of challenges after the Nepal-Tibet floods
Emergency services are rushing to find survivors and treat the wounded after a devastating flash flood on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday killed more than 500 people, with over a thousand still missing. But the remote and rugged terrain, as well as the risk of further flooding from upstream lakes formed by piles of debris, make their work as delicate as it is dangerous.
Rescue teams searching for survivors of a deadly flash near the border between Nepal and Tibet were forced to stop their work on Friday after water overran the banks of a lake formed by mountains of debris upstream of the flood zone.
While rescuers were later able to resume their search, the spectre of a fresh onslaught of water rolling over those who rushed to the remote Himalayan region to help in the wake of the catastrophe hammered home the vast challenges facing the rescue teams.
Police in Nepal on Friday said at least 552 people had been killed in the disaster. Chinese authorities on Friday raised the death toll in Tibet from three people to five. More than 1,400 people are still missing.
Nepalese and Chinese authorities have vowed to use all the means at their disposal to help those affected.

The overflowing “barrier lake” is one of two bodies of water formed by the torrents of mud and rubble carried away by the flood, according to an official with Nepal’s Disaster Management Authority. The official added that both lakes would continue to pose a flood risk until the water had fully drained – particularly in light of the torrential rains that are expected in coming days.
Simon Cook, a glaciologist at the University of Dundee, said the risk of further flooding looked all too real.
“This dam is just made of loose rock and mud and so on, it's not a carefully engineered dam that you might have for a reservoir or a hydropower project – it’s just loose debris holding back presumably many million cubic metres of water,” he said. “And the worry is that as more water enters that lake, it either overpowers the dam because the dam is just not strong enough to hold it, or it overtops the dam and cuts a notch through the dam material. And then once it starts cutting into that dam, the whole thing could be released.”
For rescuers locked in a race against time to recover as many survivors as possible, the conditions are far from ideal.
“I would definitely classify this as one of the more complicated rescue missions there is,” said Daniel Nohrstedt, a specialist in crisis management following natural disasters at the University of Uppsala in Sweden.
Researchers said the region’s rugged terrain and the wet forecast are first and foremost among the steep obstacles that rescue crews must grapple with.
“We are dealing with just about the most difficult terrain in the world for this kind of rescue," said David Alexander, a specialist in emergency response planning at University College, London.
The mountainous region was hard enough to access even before the disaster, but now the ways in and out of the area are almost impassable; Wednesday’s floods have swept away most of the bridges and clogged the roads with deep banks of mud.
Deploying excavators capable of clearing the widespread debris, for example, would run the risk of triggering further landslides, disaster management specialists said.
“Helicopter is probably the only way,” said Alexander. Nepal’s disaster management authority on Friday said that more than 3,000 people had been airlifted from the disaster zone by helicopter.
But going in by air is not easy either. The sheer amount of mud and water in the most seriously hit areas makes landing difficult, and the weather is hardly likely to make it any better.
The flash flood came at the height of the region’s monsoon season, which means that heavy rains could thunder down at any minute from a sky that rarely clears. Nohrstedt said that even airborne operations were dangerous under these conditions – not just for rescue crews trying to land in the worst-hit areas, but for survivors being evacuated by air.
“Even going in with a helicopter in this area, you run a big risk that the helicopter will go down,” he said. “Especially if the weather conditions are bad.”
Race against time

Title: Fact-Check: Unrelated & AI Visuals Falsely Linked to Recent Nepal Floods

Amid the floods in Nepal, videos are being shared claiming to show the conditions in Nepal.
- A video claiming to show a street getting wiped out by the flash floods in Nepal, and one of a herd of elephants being swept away by the Nepal floods and reaching Uttar Pradesh, are a few of the videos that are going viral.
- The viral video of the elephants was shared by news organisations Mirror Now and CNN-News18.
How did we find out?:
1. Video 1: The first video claims to show a herd of wild elephants that were swept away by the floods in Nepal, reaching Uttar Pradesh.
- We ran a reverse image search on the first video using Google Lens and found a report by Hindi news publication Dainik Bhaskar that shared a video with similar visuals to the viral video.
- According to the report, wild elephants that were coming from the Gerua River reached the gate at the Chaudhary Charan Singh Ghaghra Barrage in Bahraich district of Uttar Pradesh due to strong currents in the river.
- The report also notes that the Forest Range Officer said that since the area is adjacent to the elephant corridor, they often move there.
- After conducting a keyword search, we found another report on the same incident.
- According to The Times of India article, five wild elephants were trapped in the currents of the Kaudiyala river on 25 August 2026.
- They were rescued by the range officer and a team of forest officers.
- This incident occurred on the 25th, while the Nepal flash floods started on 26 August 2026.
- This proves that the video is unrelated to the Nepal floods.
Video 2: The second video shows a street being wiped out by the floods.
- We ran a reverse image search on the first video using Google Lens and could not find any credible sources sharing it.
- Following this, we ran the video through Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, which flagged it as 99 percent likely to be AI-generated.
- Upon close observation, we observed some irregularities.
- The vehicles and buildings collapse unrealistically as the water moves over them.
- We also observed that the trees fall unnaturally. Some of the trees and structures appear and morph out of nowhere.
- This proves that the video was AI-generated.
Conclusion: Neither of the videos shows actual footage of the Nepal floods.

Title: Murder trial jury sees footage of accused stomping on partner's head

In short:
Lindsay Kennedy has faced trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court this week for the alleged murder of his former partner, Colleen Bradshaw.
Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Mr Kennedy violently assaulting Ms Bradshaw days before her death in Royal Darwin Hospital from "blunt force head trauma".
What's next?
The jury is expected to begin deliberations next week.
A 47-year-old man has faced trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court this week for the alleged murder of his former partner in Katherine two years ago.
Lindsay Kennedy was charged with Colleen Bradshaw's murder in November 2024, four months after her death at the Royal Darwin Hospital from a traumatic brain injury on July 17.
During the hearing this week, jurors were played footage from two CCTV cameras on Railway Terrace in Katherine's town centre, showing Mr Kennedy punching Ms Bradshaw six days earlier on July 11, and stomping on her head after she fell to the ground.
The footage showed Mr Kennedy walking away twice, before returning to kick the 36-year-old in the head and chest, telling her to "get the f*** out of my life".
He was then seen in the footage leaving her lying on the footpath, crying out in pain.
In her closing address this afternoon, Crown prosecutor Deborah Mandie told the jury they could infer Mr Kennedy's murderous intent from his actions captured in the CCTV footage.
"First he runs intentionally, directly toward the deceased, unprovoked, with fist raised," she said.
"The accused punches her in the head and face and then stomps, and then kicks her head twice more.
"This is not an impulsive, isolated action."
In reply, defence barrister David Hallowes SC told the jury they could use "whatever adjectives you want" to describe his client's actions.
But he said the fact of his assault against Ms Bradshaw, causing her death, did not establish his intent to kill her, and therefore his guilt for the crime of murder.
"She's not dying at that time, you'd think if that's what he wanted — her to die — he would keep on going until he achieved that," he said.
"Say whatever you will about the assault, it was not an intention to kill."
Mr Hallowes told the jury a guilty verdict to the alternate offence of committing a violent act causing death would be most appropriate, while also accepting that negligent manslaughter might be proven.
Deceased put on bus to Darwin
The court heard Ms Bradshaw and her sister had called Triple Zero (000) four times in the days after the assault before she was eventually seen by hospital staff.
The audio from the first Triple Zero call was also played to the jury, with Ms Bradshaw heard telling the operator "I'm injured" and "I need to press charges".
She was visited the next morning by police, but did not go to hospital against the advice of her sister, who called Triple Zero twice more that afternoon.
The court heard it was only after the fourth Triple Zero call on July 12, in which Ms Bradshaw said she felt "heavy in my head" and "it's killing me", that an ambulance was sent to take her to the Katherine District Hospital.
But given what the court heard were "unremarkable" vital signs, Ms Mandie said the focus was on an unrelated wound to Ms Bradshaw's wrist that had become infected.
She was kept in hospital overnight before being put on a Greyhound bus to Darwin on July 13, where she presented to Royal Darwin Hospital and was again assessed and given antibiotics to treat her infected wound.
The following day, police attempted to take a statement from Ms Bradshaw, but were told she was too sick.
Ms Mandie told jurors it was another day later, early on July 15, after days of complaining of dizziness, blurred vision and vomiting, that Ms Bradshaw was assessed for "urgent cardiology concerns".
By that afternoon she had been given a CT scan and placed in the hospital's intensive care unit.
On July 16, her family was told that she would not survive and she was declared dead the next day.
In her testimony earlier this week, forensic pathologist Salona Roopan, who performed Ms Bradshaw's autopsy, told the court she determined her cause of death to be "blunt force head trauma and consequences thereof".
She said a blunt force trauma suffered by Ms Bradshaw approximately seven to fourteen days prior to her death had started a slow bleed inside her skull.
"Because it's a closed space, the pressure rises because there's more blood than there should be," she said.
"And now there's nowhere for that blood to go, so it starts pushing the brain in order to make space for itself to accumulate."
The court heard that by the time she died, the bleeding around Ms Bradshaw's brain had displaced it by almost a centimetre.
Justice Peter Barr is expected to give his instructions to jurors on Monday before they retire to begin their deliberations.

ATLANTA — After a tumultuous and secretive process, the Georgia Public Service Commission staff approved the contract between Georgia Power and OpenAI to power a 3.2 gigawatt hyperscale data center planned for Effingham County — without a direct vote from the commission itself.
In response, Sierra Club and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy released the following statements:
“Thanks to the public outcry against Georgia Power’s secrecy, the Public Service Commission took the first steps to bring the OpenAI development out of the dark. While this agreement is a step toward protecting ratepayers and increasing transparency, it is not enough. The Commissioners at the PSC must be empowered to weigh-in on future contract decisions,” said Hannah Baker, Organizer with Sierra Club’s Georgia Chapter. “The people of Georgia are angry at what they see as a reckless rush to build A.I. data centers with no regard to the communities they impact. We cannot allow more backroom deals that benefit Georgia Power’s profit-driven loyalty to data centers to steamroll public accountability.”
“Instead of a transparent review by elected Commissioners, PSC staff and Georgia Power co-released a letter that appears designed to alleviate the public’s concerns about whether this huge data center will raise everyone’s electric bills. But instead of providing answers, this letter leaves key questions unanswered: how is Georgia Power calculating the cost to serve these data centers, and what protections are in place for a contract of this size in the event the data center leaves or requires less power and Georgia Power isn’t able to backfill that load?” said Maggie Shober, Research Director at the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE). “I appreciate that the PSC staff are in a difficult position in reviewing these contracts. It is up to the Commission itself to update this process to provide transparency and accountability to the public.”

Title: SoftBank seeks another $10 billion loan for OpenAI stake funding

SoftBank Group Corp. is seeking a $10 billion loan, as it looks for more funding to help refinance debt used for its investment in US tech giant OpenAI, according to people familiar with the matter.
The interest margin on the two-year facility would be around 275 basis point over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate, and Mizuho Bank Ltd. is the mandated lead arranger and bookrunner, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the matter is private.
The loan would add to SoftBank’s flurry of recent debt financing activities tied to its bet on OpenAI, including a potential bond sale of as much as $20 billion, despite concerns about growing credit risks in the artificial intelligence sector. SoftBank, founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, is slated to invest close to $65 billion in OpenAI by October.
Proceeds of the loan could partly be used to repay a $40 billion bridge loan secured earlier this year for the OpenAI investments, the people said. Commitments are due Aug. 31 and banks are already in talks to join, the people added.
The International Financing Review reported news of the deal earlier this week.
SoftBank is also looking at tapping the bond market for additional funding. It’s considering $10 billion to $20 billion offering to help refinance the bridge loan, and it’s planning a record ¥1 trillion ($6.3 billion) retail bond sale in its home market for its investment commitments to OpenAI.
The company earlier this month also secured a $10 billion loan backed by its OpenAI stake, which includes covenants that may require it to post cash or repay early.
SoftBank and Mizuho declined to comment.
SoftBank’s borrowings come as US tech firms are planning to pour trillions of dollars into data centers and other AI infrastructure in the coming years. Companies have already borrowed more than $410 billion so far this year for such facilities and other AI investments in the bond markets alone, according to data compiled by Bloomberg News.

Title: Google data center deal gives Texas farmer 60 days to leave 600 rented acres

Standing near the Haskell County border in West Texas, fourth-generation farmer Cheyenne Buerger can see industrial cranes building a huge Google facility just over four miles to the northeast. Until recently, part of that same horizon was farmland he worked himself. After farming thousands of acres with his family for more than a century, Buerger was forced to give up 600 acres of rented farmland when his landlord suddenly sold the property to a developer clearing the site for the tech giant. The eviction gave the local farmer very little time to harvest his remaining crops and leave the land. "When I explained I had a crop on it, they said 'You can finish it, but that's it,'" Buerger said. "'You've got to be done in 60 days, and you're out." Losing the land near Haskell has taken away a large part of Buerger's local farming operation. Along with his family's 6,000 acres, where they grow cotton, wheat and milo, the rented fields gave the family more flexibility for crop rotations and livestock management. "It makes me feel a little threatened just from losing land to data centers," Buerger said. "We can't compete with that."
Corporate expansion across rural Texas
The loss of farmland to technology projects is becoming more common across Texas, according to an investigation by The Texas Tribune. As major technology companies expand artificial intelligence and cloud computing, developers are moving into rural counties looking for large, flat and relatively cheap areas of land. Data from the Pew Research Center shows that about 67 per cent of data centres in the United States are located in rural areas. In Texas, low taxes and large amounts of available land have long attracted major industries, but the current growth of data centres has reached new levels. An analysis by The Texas Tribune found 335 operating data centres across Texas, with at least 248 more either planned or under construction. The fast conversion of farmland into large server campuses is causing concern among farmers who are increasingly competing with wealthy technology companies for land and other important resources, including groundwater and electricity.
Growing pressure on farmland
The expansion comes at a difficult time for Texas agriculture. The industry produces more than $963 billion in total economic activity and generates nearly $15 billion in annual exports, according to state production figures cited in the report. State officials have also criticised the choice of farmland for some of these projects. Speaking at a public forum on rural industrial development organised by The Texas Tribune in Granbury, Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller warned that turning fertile soil into technology sites could permanently reduce the state's ability to produce food. "They're building them on our most valuable, most fertile farmland," said Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller. "Once our farmland is gone and paved over, we'll never farm it again." The amount of land needed for some of these projects is enormous. Three major developments, Project Matador in the Panhandle, Project Pacifico in Pecos County and Project Meta in El Paso, are expected to cover at least 16,000 acres combined. That is roughly equal to 12,000 American football fields.
Huge projects, huge energy needs
In Hereford, about 50 miles southwest of Amarillo, Google outlined plans for its multi-phase Project Roman during a public community meeting. Local farmer Darren Grotegut attended the meeting and learned that the first phase alone would use 3,700 acres for computing facilities. More land would be needed for solar and wind projects to provide electricity. Grotegut estimated that all four phases could eventually cover more than 180,000 acres. To reduce the large amount of water needed to cool the computer equipment, project representatives said some nearby farmland could be converted into native grasslands to help protect local aquifers. The pressure on rural land is not limited to data centres. Clean energy monitoring company Cleanview says 240 utility-scale solar farms are now operating on rural Texas land. By 2024, about 1.5 million acres of former farmland across the state had been converted to solar energy production. For farmers such as Buerger, the future of tenant farming in West Texas looks increasingly uncertain. He still hauls cotton seed across his remaining pastures to feed cattle while construction crews put up steel frames on the fields he once rented. As investors and energy developers continue buying large connected areas of land across Jones and Haskell counties, family farmers have fewer options for finding replacement acreage. Rising land prices linked to industrial development are also making it harder for them to compete. Across the region, farming communities are facing lasting changes in how land, water and electricity are used.

Title: Investments in co-located solar-plus-storage reach $25 billion in H1, says BloombergNEF

Investments in co-located solar-plus-storage reach $25 billion in H1, says BloombergNEF
Global investment in renewable energy reached $327.5 billion (€281 billion) in the first half of 2026, virtually unchanged from the previous six months but 21% below the record set in the second half of 2024.
Data from BloombergNEF (BNEF) show that renewable energy deployment remains on track despite regulatory changes in key markets, including the United States and China. Investment, however, is increasingly shifting toward assets that offer greater flexibility in managing revenues.
Storage drives hybrid projects
Financing for standalone utility-scale solar fell more sharply than investment in onshore wind. Investment in standalone solar PV declined 20% year on year to $75.4 billion (€64.7 billion), its lowest level since the solar investment boom began in 2021.
Growing revenue uncertainty, driven by solar price cannibalization, curtailment and grid congestion, is pushing investors and developers toward more flexible project configurations.
Against this backdrop, co-located solar-plus-storage projects attracted a record $25 billion (€21.5 billion) in investment in the first half of 2026. The figure was nearly double the total recorded in the second half of 2025 and three times the amount invested in the first half of that year. The United States and Australia led investment in the segment.
US accelerates ahead of incentive expiration
The United States was the second-largest market for renewable energy investment, behind China but ahead of the European Union, recording 54% year-on-year growth. Developers accelerated project financing to meet tax credit deadlines and respond to surging electricity demand, driven in part by data centers.
Solar investment rose 41% to a record $45.8 billion (€39.3 billion), while wind investment reached $13.8 billion, more than double the previous year’s figure. Projects that remain eligible for tax credits could sustain construction activity in the short term, with the final installations scheduled through 2030.
European onshore wind holds firm
Global wind investment totaled $92.3 billion, down 27% year on year. Offshore wind was particularly hard hit, with investment plunging 72% amid poor auction results, higher capital and financing costs and a shrinking pipeline of projects likely to reach financial close.
Onshore wind investment declined by a more moderate 4% to $80.7 billion. Europe, however, bucked the trend, with Germany, Romania and Serbia all recording record investment levels following recent auctions.
China accounted for just one-quarter of global investment, down from more than half in 2022, following reforms to its electricity market. By contrast, Vietnam quadrupled its investment, while investment across Southeast Asia surpassed $12 billion. Nigeria increased investment in distributed solar and storage, Central Asia maintained investment above $4 billion, and Brazil helped push global biofuel investment to $7.7 billion.
BloombergNEF expects new renewable energy installations in 2026 to fall below 2025 levels, marking the first year-on-year decline in more than a decade. It expects growth to resume in 2027.

Title: ‘Environment of FIRs harmful for India’: ABP journalist booked after report on Pune college

ABP Majha journalist Mandar Gonjari’s interview with a student ahead of Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event on a Pune campus triggered a political row and a campus clash. Three FIRs have been filed. Gonjari denies the allegations.
“Such an environment of FIRs against journalists is wrong for them and not just them but for the country. It is harmful,” says ABP Majha journalist Mandar Gonjari.
The journalist in Pune has been named in an FIR after a dispute over a single student’s scholarship grievance escalated into a campus clash between rival student groups and a legal case against him. Both the FIR and the journalist now offer opposing accounts of who pressured that student to change her story.
Gonjari had on August 20 interviewed students at the College of Engineering Pune Technological University about their plans to attend Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s “Chhatron Ki Goonj” programme on August 22. Among them was Sampada Pramod Bade, a student admitted under the orphan quota, who told him she hadn’t received her scholarship for three years and was wrongly charged fees under the general category. After Gonjari’s report aired, Congress’s media cell used a clip from it to counter a claim by Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis – he had said that students attending were from institutes run by Congress leaders.
Gonjari alleges that once this happened, ABVP activists pressured Bade to publicly retract her comments, to say he had forced the interview and that her scholarship complaint wasn’t genuine. In a video released by Bade after the ABP Majha report, the student said, “We were actually manipulated and pressure was created due to which I said it… This was wrong. So I apologise to the college.” In another video posted by BJP, Bade said, “Please free our campus from political activities.”
As the controversy over the claim and the counter-claim grew, there was a confrontation on campus between ABVP and NSUI on August 21. And three FIRs were filed. In the first, an ABVP member accused the NSUI and Congress of assaulting ABVP members and pressuring the girl student to make a statement. In the second, the Youth Congress alleged that Bade was locked up in the COEP hostel by the ABVP and Congress workers were assaulted. In the third, the COEP accused the NSUI and Congress of trespassing on premises and posting the defamatory statement by Bade. This third FIR also claimed that Gonjari entered the hostel premises without permission.
Bade’s phone remained switched off. Newslaundry has sent her a questionnaire. This report will be updated if a response is received.
The Pune Union of Working Journalists has condemned the action against Gonjari and submitted a request to the Commissioner of Police, demanding his removal from the case.
Gonjari, on his part, denies all the allegations and maintains that he did not even enter the hostel. He was also not the only journalist to have interviewed Bade.
India Today’s Pune Bureau Chief Omkar Wable tweeted, “It’s interesting that the same girl I interviewed was talking about how she hasn’t received her orphan scholarship amount and was also raising concerns about the fee hike at the college.”
Gonjari: ‘Every party wants control’
On Thursday, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said in Nagpur that students from Congress-affiliated colleges would attend Gandhi’s Pune programme.
As per an Indian Express report, he said, “Instead of limiting his interactions to young people in colleges run by Congress leaders, Rahul Gandhi should interact with youth across the board. I have information that the Congress has invited only those students who are from colleges run by the Congress leaders. There are directions to Congress leaders to register only such students. Nevertheless, they are also our students.”
Gonjari then went to COEP, where he interviewed seven students, four women and three men, about why they planned to attend the event and what issues they intended to raise there.
The journalist said several students raised concerns about scholarships and hostel infrastructure. Sampada Pramod Bade, he said, spoke about not receiving an orphanage-category scholarship for three years, while another student spoke about problems in the hostel, including terrace leakages. He also asked the students whether they were affiliated with any student organisation, to which they said they were not. (Gonjari’s interview with Bade is 0:55 seconds onwards in the ABP Majha report.)
The report was broadcast on August 21. Gonjari said the Congress media cell subsequently used a clip of Fadnavis’s statement alongside footage of him asking students whether they had any political affiliations, presenting it as a rebuttal to the chief minister’s claim about who would attend Gandhi’s programme.
Gonjari alleged that after the video circulated, ABVP members went to the college and pressured Bade to say that he had forced her to give the interview and that she was not actually going to Gandhi’s event. The journalist added that the student group pressured Bade to say that she did not actually have any scholarship-related issues.
Gonjari alleged that this was followed by a tussle between ABVP and NSUI members inside the COEP premises, which led to a lathi-charge and cases being registered.
Gonjari won the Ramnath Goenka Excellence in Journalism Awards presented in March 2025 for his reporting on how an undertrial allegedly operated a synthetic drug racket from his hospital bed in Pune.
Gonjari said he believed the FIR was connected to the circulation of his interview by the Congress media cell. He said neither the police nor any political party had pressured him to delete the report, and that his newsroom and editors had supported him.
He also said the episode reflected a wider problem for journalists in the country. “Such an environment of FIRs against journalists is wrong for them and not just them but for the country. It is harmful. If the correct information is not reaching the public, it is wrong. Clean and true journalism is important for this country,” he said.
“Every political party, be it BJP or Congress, wants control over journalists. But to what degree can you go for that control, political parties really need to think about this,” he added.
‘Interview recorded in front of college canteen’
The FIR, registered at Shivajinagar police station, names 100 to 150 Congress and NSUI workers and others and invokes provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita relating to unlawful assembly, rioting, criminal trespass, criminal intimidation, intentional insult and defamation, besides Sections 37(3) and 135 of the Maharashtra Police Act.
The complaint was filed by the chief administrative officer of COEP’s hostel department, who was authorised by the university to lodge the complaint.
The complaint alleges that NSUI and Congress workers entered the hostel premises without permission on August 21, pushed security guards and students, shouted slogans and created an “atmosphere of fear” among hostel residents. It also alleges that an ABP Majha journalist entered the hostel premises without permission and states that there was a “legal complaint” against him.
Gonjari, however, told Newslaundry that the interviews were recorded outside the college canteen in an open area during daylight. “We recorded the interview in front of the college canteen space. It was an open space and in daylight,” Gonjari said. The interviews uploaded on ABP Majha’s YouTube channel show they were recorded in an open space.
He added that other reporters were also present. “One was from Aaj Tak, who interviewed students as well. There was another channel as well. Even security was present there, and we were not stopped,” the journalist said.
Former PUWJ president Brijmohan Patil also took to X and claimed that Gonjari had not gone to the women’s hostel for an interview. “#Pune: Some people are blatantly lying that ABP Majha's bureau chief Mandar Gonjari #COEP went to the women's hostel at night for an interview. Look at the photo below. That's the COEP campus. Boys were also present with the girls in this discussion. Don't support false things,” he wrote. (sic)
The FIR naming Gonjari alleges that on August 19, NSUI workers prepared and circulated a video using Bade’s name “against her wishes”, claiming that the university had improperly charged her fees despite her admission under the orphan quota. The complaint says the university later learnt that it had “spoken incorrectly” and that Bade subsequently met the vice-chancellor along with other students.
The complaint further says that on August 21, between 7 pm and 7:30 pm, students admitted under the orphan quota met the hostel administration and said their demands had been accepted.
It alleged that around 7:45 pm, 15 to 20 NSUI workers forcibly opened the hostel gate, pushed security guards and entered the premises. It then alleges that another 100 to 150 NSUI workers gathered inside, shouted slogans, and abused and assaulted students.
The FIR does not allege that Gonjari was involved in the purported violence or slogan-shouting attributed to the Congress and NSUI workers.
Cops say ‘investigating’
ABVP has alleged that the COEP girl student’s video exposed the Congress and NSUI so their workers allegedly barged into COEP premises and caused a ruckus.
Speaking to Newslaundry, ABVP Pune Secretary Radheya Bahegavankar denied the allegation about pressurising Bade into changing her statement. He said that it was NSUI workers who had forced students to give statements regarding attending Gandhi’s event. He further alleged 400-500 NSUI workers entered COEP premises and attacked students. He said, “Sampada, herself, recorded the video and sent her statement. ABVP has no relations with the student. I am not aware whether the ABP Majha journalist entered the hostel or not.”
Akshay Jain, chairman of Maharashtra State Youth Congress-Media and Communication Department, who is also named in the FIR, told Newslaundry: “NSUI workers campaigned at COEP and other colleges to inform students about Gandhi’s event. Students told us about their issues and also mentioned the Orphan Scholarship. Gonjari interviewed these students - not just Sampada, but others as well who were facing issues with the scholarship. ABP Majha’s report went viral, following which the Maharashtra government released the scholarship money.”
“Later, ABVP pressured the students to change their statements and claim that NSUI had forced them to give bytes about the scholarship issue. If you see the news report containing the students’ interviews, it was very raw and organic. NSUI then demanded a conversation with the administration. We also asked to speak with Sampada, but that was not allowed. ABVP then got FIRs registered against our group. The first FIR was registered on a complaint by ABVP, while the second was registered by the college administration, which also alleged that the ABP Majha journalist had trespassed.”
“Please see the CCTV footage…we did not engage in any violence. ABVP attacked us first and also indulged in sloganeering. Three of our members were injured. This is a way of misusing power and suppressing the media.”
Police inspector Amar Kalange of Shivajinagar police station, where the FIR naming the journalist was filed, told Newslaundry, “The FIR has been registered as per the complainant’s statement. It only says that the complaint is also against an ABP Majha journalist. The police are investigating the matter.”

Title: Trump Dismisses NATO Attack Fears After CIA Chief’s Moscow Trip

US President Donald Trump told reporters that he does not believe Moscow will attack a NATO nation amid rising concerns that Russian President Vladimir Putin will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test the Western alliance’s resolve.
Trump on August 27 told reporters in the Oval Office that he had engaged in "good talks" with Putin and that "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory." He did not specify when those talks were held.
"I am not concerned...at all. There is no problem," Trump was quoted earlier as saying by news publication Axios when asked about a possible Russian provocation against a NATO state.
The remarks come as the Kremlin, at the same time, dismissed as "scare stories" reports in the US media suggesting Moscow could attack NATO and following a surprise visit by the CIA director to Moscow.
NATO Article 5 Assurances
Western European security has long been tied to NATO's mutual defense clause, Article 5, which states that an attack on one member nation constitutes an attack on all.
Many Western leaders and officials have expressed concerns over Trump's commitment to the military alliance. Trump has at times put into question a possible US response to an attack on a member state, while at other times reaffirming support for NATO.
A letter seen by RFE/RL reveals growing concern about Russian aggression in the Baltic states, speaking of a "deteriorating security environment" amid an "increased frequency of airspace violations and drone incursions."
The letter was sent to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and signed by the three Baltic European commissioners, Kaja Kallas, Andrius Kubilius, and Valdis Dombrovskis, as well as the Polish and Finnish commissioners.
Dated July 30, the letter was one of a series of alarm bells sounded about Russian aggression over the course of the summer that culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe's surprise visit to Moscow on August 25.
Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to urge the Kremlin against escalating with US allies -- particularly Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania -- sources briefed about the visit confirmed to RFE/RL on August 26.
'Every Six Months'
Axios quoted Trump as denying Ratcliffe had issued such a warning to the Russians.
"Ratcliffe sees his Russian counterpart once every six months or once every year. They have a very good relationship. There was no message and there was nothing unusual," Trump said.
But when asked about the matter later by reporters in the Oval Office, Trump appeared to back off, saying: "I don't want to comment on that, but they're not going to attack [NATO]."
The New York Times, citing current and former officials, said Ratcliffe gave his counterpart a bleak assessment of the state of the Russia's war against Ukraine and to urge the Kremlin to reach a deal before its military and economic situation becomes worse.
The Wall Street Journal earlier cited US intelligence as stating Russia may test NATO resolve with a limited incursion as early as this fall.
Baltic diplomats who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity confirmed there was additional intelligence during the summer of Russian false-flag operations but no indication about an imminent conventional attack.
They were also keen to point out that such operations might not be limited to the Baltics, a concern reinforced by recent cases of alleged or suspected Russian involvement in assassination attempts, fires, and drone incursions in several NATO countries, including Germany, Poland, and Slovakia.
NATO Members Pressed
Separately, a senior Pentagon official on August 27 pressed NATO allies to outline how they were answering US demands that they take more responsibility for Europe's defense as Washington reviews its force levels on the continent.
The US administration under Trump has ignited fears among allies that the US could cut back its forces in Europe following a six-month review that began in July.
"The spirit that we come in is obviously one...of consultation, of engagement. We want to hear from our allies," US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said during a visit for talks at NATO's headquarters in Brussels.
Washington has sent out a questionnaire asking European countries to explain their efforts in taking the forefront in protecting the continent.
"We're actually having a kind of down-to-business conversation about how we go forward together in a world in which Europe, which is obviously a very wealthy continent, can and is taking primary responsibility for its own conventional defense," Colby said.
By RFE/RL

Title: Amazon Nears 1 GW of Wind Power in Sweden With Four New Deals

Amazon has expanded Germany’s largest-ever power purchase agreement (PPA), signed in June, and announced another four deals to buy power from four wind farms in Sweden as the e-commerce giant and other electricity-intensive hyperscalers look to power their rising AI computing and data center needs with carbon-free electricity.
Amazon on Friday highlighted the signing of a PPA to purchase 600 megawatts (MW) of carbon-free electricity from the Gennaker offshore wind farm in the German Baltic Sea. By agreeing to purchase this energy, Amazon will give developer Skyborn Renewables the financial certainty needed to move forward with construction of the project.
The Gennaker offshore wind farm will be located off the coast of northeastern Germany and, once operational, is expected to generate enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than one million German households annually, Amazon said.
Moreover, Amazon also announced four PPAs in Sweden to purchase power from four new wind energy projects in the Scandinavian country.
With the new deals for wind power purchases, Amazon’s total carbon-free energy capacity in the country is closing in on 1 gigawatt (GW), equivalent to powering more than 350,000 Swedish households every year.
The four farms in Sweden are being developed by Eolus AB and OX2 AB, Amazon said in comments on the PPAs emailed to Bloomberg.
With the new agreements, Amazon has now invested in a total of nine utility-scale wind energy projects in Sweden.
“The world needs more energy, and it needs that energy to be carbon-free, reliable, and affordable for everyone,” said Gulfem Toygar, country manager for Amazon Sweden.
“Our wind energy investments in Sweden are part of how we're helping to bring more carbon-free energy to the grid.”
Amazon and other giant hyperscalers are looking for carbon-free power – where available – to power their soaring electricity demand.
Last year, electricity demand from data centers jumped by 17%, and that of AI-focused data centers surged even faster, soaring by 50%, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in a report in April. These surges in AI-driven power demand vastly outpaced the 3% growth in global electricity demand.

Title: Alibaba’s (BABA) Big AI Bet Comes With A Big Price Tag

On August 20, Alibaba (NYSE:BABA) reported fiscal first-quarter results that read like two different companies stitched into one filing. Revenue rose 9% year over year to 269 billion yuan, powered by a cloud business finally hitting its stride. But net income cratered 75% to 10.4 billion yuan, and free cash flow ran to an outflow of 44.7 billion yuan. It's the story of a company choosing to sacrifice near-term profit for a much bigger bet on artificial intelligence.
The Cloud Business Finally Delivers
Alibaba Cloud's external revenue grew 45% year over year, a 22-quarter high, and the acceleration wasn't just a top-line number. Adjusted EBITA for the AI Cloud and Compute Services segment jumped 133% to 5.6 billion yuan, a sign that the business is starting to spread its fixed costs across a bigger revenue base rather than simply growing for growth's sake. AI-related products, which carry higher margins than the rest of the cloud portfolio, meaningfully notched a 12th straight quarter of triple-digit growth and now make up 35% of external cloud revenue, with an annual run rate topping 49.5 billion yuan.
Behind that growth is a bet on owning the whole AI stack rather than renting pieces of it. Qwen, Alibaba's family of open-source models, has been downloaded more than 3 billion times and spawned over 300,000 derivative models, a flywheel in which outside developers build on Qwen and then need Alibaba Cloud's infrastructure to run what they've built. Title: Bombay High Court Upholds Goa Municipalities Ordinance, Sets January 2 Deadline for Elections

The Bombay High Court on Thursday (August 27, 2026) upheld the validity of the Goa Municipalities (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, while directing the Goa State Election Commission (GSEC) to complete elections to 11 municipal councils by January 2, 2027.
A division bench of Justice Valmiki Menezes and Justice Hiten Venegavkar made it clear that the Constitutional mandate under Article 243U must be followed, regardless of administrative convenience or proximity to State Assembly elections.
“No Government has a Constitutional entitlement to choose a politically convenient date for an election whose periodicity is fixed by the Constitution,” the bench observed in its August 25 ruling. “No Legislature can proceed on the assumption that enactment of a new electoral requirement automatically supplies additional constitutional time for its implementation.”
The 232-page judgment, authored by Justice Venegavkar, addressed a batch of petitions challenging the ordinance introduced in April 2026, which substantially changed the process of delimitation and reservation of municipal wards.
The petitioners argued that the ordinance was introduced after the GSEC had commenced preparations for elections. The existing municipalities’ terms were set to expire in March and May 2026. The petitioners contended that the ordinance forced a restart of the entire election process, delaying it further.
The GSEC stated that it could not proceed without proper consultations with the State on delimitations and other matters. The government argued that Article 243U does not freeze the State’s powers to amend election laws.
While upholding the ordinance’s validity, the bench ordered that Article 243U provisions must be followed scrupulously.
“The Commission was constitutionally obliged, once the Ordinance intervened, to ensure that the transition from the old regime to the new one caused the least possible additional loss of time,” the court said. “A valid change in the statutory foundation justified such repetition as the new law genuinely required, it did not justify treating every prior act as wasted work.”
The court emphasised that the State Election Commission occupies an independent Constitutional position. “That independence requires constitutional distance from executive convenience, but it equally requires cooperation where the statute legitimately assigns interdependent functions to different authorities.”
Addressing concerns that the ordinance was introduced to align civic elections with State Assembly polls, the bench directed that the municipal election process must be completed by January 2, irrespective of Assembly election schedules.
“If additional personnel, vehicles, security arrangements or other resources are required to ensure that the municipal process is completed before the Assembly election machinery becomes fully engaged, it is for the State Government to make those arrangements,” the court stated. “An anticipated future demand upon the same administrative machinery cannot legitimise continuation of an existing breach of Article 243U.”
The court further observed that Article 243U operates through multiple institutions including the State Legislature, the State Government, the State Election Commission, and specialised bodies performing antecedent functions concerning reservation or empirical inquiry.
“Their functions are distinct, but the constitutional result is indivisible: an elected Municipality must be democratically reconstituted within the period prescribed by the Constitution,” the bench noted. “No authority can therefore treat compliance with Article 243U as the responsibility of another.”
The bench ruled that neither the State nor the Commission can invoke statutory change as a complete answer to constitutional default. “The Commission cannot say that because the statute requires consultation, empirical data or other action by different authorities, its constitutional obligation remains suspended until those authorities act.”
With these directions, the court disposed of the petitions.
